questions.response: write the answer and show the required work
questions.prompt: System A: x + 2y = 7 and 3x - y = 7. System B: x + 2y = 7 and 7x = 21, where 7x = 21 is the first equation plus 2 times the second. Show that every solution of A solves B and every solution of B solves A. Then give the solution.
questions.prompt_markup:
System A: x + 2y = 7 and 3x - y = 7. System B: x + 2y = 7 and 7x = 21, where 7x = 21 is the first equation plus 2 times the second.
Show that every solution of A solves B and every solution of B solves A. Then give the solution.
questions.required_method: A to B: a solution of A makes both equations true, so adding x + 2y = 7 and 2(3x - y) = 14 gives 7x = 21. B to A: from 7x = 21 and x + 2y = 7, subtracting gives 6x - 2y = 14, so 3x - y = 7. The kept equation x + 2y = 7 is in both systems.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both directions and the solution. Check: 3 + 4 = 7 and 9 - 2 = 7.

questions.skill: Prove that replacing an equation by its sum with a multiple of the other gives an equivalent system, in both directions
questions.standard_level: Algebra I. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra I, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.response: write the answer and show the required work
questions.prompt: Let P = c and Q = d be the two equations of a system (P and Q are expressions in x and y). Prove that the system P = c and Q + kP = d + kc has exactly the same solutions, for any number k.
questions.prompt_markup: Let P = c and Q = d be the two equations of a system (P and Q are expressions in x and y). Prove that the system P = c and Q + kP = d + kc has exactly the same solutions, for any number k.
questions.correct_answer: The two systems have the same solutions.
questions.required_method: If (x, y) makes P = c and Q = d true, then Q + kP = d + kc (adding equal amounts), so it solves the new system. Conversely, if P = c and Q + kP = d + kc, subtracting kP = kc gives Q = d. So the solution sets are equal.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both directions, each with its reason.

questions.skill: Prove that replacing an equation by its sum with a multiple of the other gives an equivalent system, in both directions
questions.standard_level: Algebra I. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra I, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Why must the new system keep one of the original equations unchanged? Give an example.
questions.prompt_markup: Why must the new system keep one of the original equations unchanged? Give an example.
questions.correct_answer: The kept equation is needed to recover the replaced one. For example, replacing both x + y = 2 and x - y = 0 with their sum 2x = 2 alone loses information: 2x = 2 has infinitely many solutions (x = 1, any y), but the system has only (1, 1).
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation with an example.
